Baire Category Theorem

This scene follows the Baire category theorem through nested intervals. Dodge the rationals one by one, and a point still remains.

Sets full of holes cannot cover everything. Choose smaller and smaller closed intervals, each dodging the next bad point. The intervals tighten onto one point belonging to no hole set. A complete space always keeps such a point.

For example, put a 📦 box inside a box, then a smaller one inside that. However small it gets, room remains at the center. Choosing the boxes to dodge rationals still leaves one point standing.

    Hence a complete metric space cannot be a countable union of nowhere dense sets.

    The intuition: each nowhere dense set leaves a "hole", and completeness traps the limit point obtained by descending through those holes inside the space.

Show proof

  1. By construction each IkI_kIk​ is a closed interval with Ik+1⊆IkI_{k+1} \subseteq I_kIk+1​⊆Ik​; when qkq_kqk​ lands in Ik−1I_{k-1}Ik−1​ we take IkI_kIk​ of one-quarter the length with qk∉Ikq_k \notin I_kqk​∈/Ik​ (if qkq_kqk​ already lies outside, Ik=Ik−1I_k = I_{k-1}Ik​=Ik−1​).

  2. The lengths tend to 000.

    Suppose no more "hits" occur after stage KKK; then In=IKI_n = I_KIn​=IK​ for all n≥Kn \ge Kn≥K and the length stays positive.

    But IKI_KIK​ has positive length, so it contains infinitely many rationals, each appearing exactly once in the enumeration — hence some qm∈IKq_m \in I_Kqm​∈IK​ has index m>Km > Km>K.

    Then Im−1=IK∋qmI_{m-1} = I_K \ni q_mIm−1​=IK​∋qm​, so stage mmm is a hit — a contradiction.

    Hits therefore occur infinitely often, and each one quarters the length, so ℓk→0\ell_k \to 0ℓk​→0.

  3. By completeness of R\mathbb{R}R (the nested interval theorem), nested closed intervals whose lengths tend to 000 intersect in exactly one point: ⋂kIk={x}\bigcap_k I_k = \{x\}⋂k​Ik​={x}. And since x∈Ikx \in I_kx∈Ik​ while qk∉Ikq_k \notin I_kqk​∈/Ik​, we have x≠qkx \ne q_kx=qk​ for every kkk.

  4. Since {qk}\{q_k\}{qk​} enumerates every rational of [0,1][0, 1][0,1], xxx is an irrational in [0,1][0, 1][0,1].

    Hence [0,1]=⋃k{qk}[0, 1] = \bigcup_k \{q_k\}[0,1]=⋃k​{qk​} — a countable union of points — is impossible, and [0,1][0, 1][0,1] is uncountable.

    This is the point-set version of Baire's theorem: a singleton is nowhere dense in R\mathbb{R}R, so [0,1][0, 1][0,1], being complete, cannot be a countable union of points without contradicting Baire.
